result.summary: Pausanias describes a temple of Artemis near an unnamed town, then the Phocian coastal town of Bulis with its temples and purple-dye industry. He moves on to Cirrha, port of Delphi, and tells how the Amphictyones, advised by Solon, destroyed it for its impiety against Apollo.

scenes.title: Temple of Artemis by Praxiteles
scenes.summary: A temple on a lofty rock holds a tall statue of Artemis by Praxiteles, with torch, quiver and dog.

scenes.title: The town of Bulis
scenes.summary: Pausanias gives the founding, distances, purple-dye trade and temples of Bulis.

scenes.title: Cirrha and its Hippodrome
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the Pythian Hippodrome, the barren plain of Cirrha, and the town's names and impiety.

scenes.title: Solon and the siege of Cirrha
scenes.summary: The Amphictyones besiege Cirrha; following the oracle and Solon's hellebore trick, they capture it.
scenes.stakes: Cirrha's people face destruction for their impiety against Apollo.

scenes.title: Temple at Cirrha
scenes.summary: Cirrha has a temple of Apollo, Artemis and Leto with Attic statues, and a small Adrastea.

alias_notes.explanation: Pausanias guesses the Bulis title 'Supreme' refers to Zeus.
Ancient name of Cirrha, used by Homer.

notable_quotes.reason: The oracle's riddling response that guided the capture of Cirrha.

analysis.text: Offences against Apollo's sanctuary bring divine punishment, and the oracle's riddle is solved by human cleverness.
The account reflects the First Sacred War (early 6th century BC), in which the Amphictyonic League destroyed Cirrha and secured Delphi's access to the sea.

fun_facts.text: Bulis was known in antiquity for purple dye from shellfish, which Pausanias notes employed most of its people.

language_notes.text: A stade was a Greek unit of length, roughly 180–185 metres, so 2 stades is about 370 metres.
"Supreme" (Hypatos) was a cult title often attached to Zeus; Pausanias guesses the god meant, since the locals do not name him.
The Taraxippus ("horse-terrifier") was a spot in the Olympia hippodrome where horses were said to panic; Pausanias treated it in his book on Elis.
Crisa is the name in Homer's Iliad and the Hymn to Apollo; Cirrha later became the usual name for the town.
The Amphictyones were the member states of the league that administered the Delphic sanctuary and could declare sacred wars.
Amphitrite, the sea goddess and wife of Poseidon, stands here for the sea itself; the oracle asks for the sea to reach Apollo's grove.
Adrastea is a goddess associated with Nemesis, who punishes excess and arrogance, which suits a town punished for impiety.

context_notes.text: Praxiteles was a famous fourth-century BC Athenian sculptor; Artemis is the goddess of hunting, often shown with a quiver, torch and hound.
Philomelus was a Phocian general who seized Delphi's sanctuary and treasure in the Third Sacred War (mid-fourth century BC).
Purple dye was made from murex shellfish and was a valuable ancient trade.
This is the First Sacred War (early sixth century BC). Solon was the Athenian statesman and lawgiver.
Hellebore is a poisonous plant used as a strong purge. This stratagem is a famous story of early chemical warfare.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias shows his rational, pious outlook, attributing fortune to the god and rejecting hero-malice explanations for horses' fear.
The oracle seems to demand the impossible, yet Solon fulfils it by a clever reading, consecrating the land to the sea's edge.
One long, flowing sentence narrates the whole trick, effect and conquest in sequence, ending with the town's new role.
